source_text: Anno quintodecimo principatus Tiberii proponit eum descendisse in ciuitatem Galilaeae Capharnaum, utique de caelo creatoris, in quod de suo ante descenderat. ecquid ergo ordinis fuerat, ut prius de suo caelo in creatoris descendens describeretur? cur enim non et ista reprehendam, quae non implent fidem ordinariae narrationis, deficientis in mendacio semper? plane semel dicta sint per quae iam alibi retractauimus: an descendens per creatorem, et quidem aduersus ipsum, potuerit ab eo admitti et inde tramitti in terram aeque ipsius. nunc autem et reliquum ordinem descensionis expostulo, tenens (descendisse) illum. uiderit enim, sicubi \'apparuisse* positum est. apparere subitum ex inopinato sapit conspectum, qui semel impegerit oculos in id, quod sine mora apparuit, descendisse autem dum fit uidetur et subicit oculos de facto. etiam ordinem facit atque ita cogit exigere, quali habitu, quali suggestu, quonam impetu uel temperamento, etiam quo in tempore diei noctisue descenderit; praeterea, quis uiderit descendentem, quis retulerit, quis adseuerauerit rem, utique nec adseueranti facile credendam. indignum denique, ut Romulus quidem ascensus sui in caelum habuerit Proculum adfirmatorem, Christus uero dei descensus de caelo sui non inuenerit adnuntiatorem, *** quasi non sic et ille ascenderit isdem mendacii scalis, sicut et iste descendit. quid autem illi cum Galilaea. si non erat creatoris, cui ista regio destinabatur ingressuro praedicationem, dicente Esaia: hoc primum bibito, cito facito, regio Zabulon et terra Nepthalim, et ceteri quimaritimam, etIordanis, Galilaea nationum. populus, qui sedetis in tenebris, uidete lumen magnum; qui habitatis terram, sedentes in umbra mortis, lumen ortum est super uos? bene autem, quod et deus Marcionis inluminator uindicatur nationum, quo magis debuerit, uel de caelo etsi descenderet, utique in Pontum potius descendere quam in Galilaeam. ceterum et loco et inluminationis opere secundum praedicationem occurrentibus Christo iam eum prophetatum incipimus agnoscere, ostendentem in primo ingressu uenisse se, non ut legem et prophetas dissolueret, sed ut potius adimpleret. hoc enim Marcion ut additum erasit. sed frustra negabit Christum dixisse quod statim fecit ex parte. prophetiam enim interim de loco adimpleuit: de caelo statim. ad synagogam. ut dici solet: \'ad quod uenimus, hoc age\\ Marcion: aufer etiam illud de euangelio: non sum missus nisi ad oues perditas domus Israhel, et: non est auferre panem filiis et dare eum canibus, ne scilicet Christus Israhelis uideatur. sufficiunt mihi facta pro dictis. detrahe uoces Christi mei: res loquentur. ecce uenit in synagogam: certe ad oues perditas domus Israhelis. ecce doctrinae suae panem prioribus offert Israhelitis: certe, ut filios praefert. ecce aliis eum nondum impertit: certe, ut canes praeterit. quibus autem magis impertisset quam extraneis creatoris, si ipse inprimis non fuisset creatoris? et tamen quomodo in synagogam potuit admitti tam repentinus, tam ignotus, cuius nemo adhuc certus de tribu, de populo, de domo, de censu denique Augusti, quem testem fidelissimum dominicae natiuitatis Romana archiua custodiunt? Meminerant certe, nisi circumcisum scirent, non admittendum in sancta sanctorum. sed etsi passim synagoga adiretur, non tamen ad docendum nisi ab optime cognito et explorato et probato iam pridem in hoc ipsum uel aliunde commendato cum hoc munere. stupebant autem omnes ad doctrinam eius. plane. quoniam, inquit, in potestate erat sermo eius, non quoniam aduersus legem et prophetas docebat. utique enim eloquium diuinum et uim et gratiam praestabat, magis exstruens quam destruens substantiam legis et prophetarum. alioquin non stuperent, sed horrerent, nec mirarentur, sed statim auersarentur destructorem legis et prophetarum, et utique inprimis alterius dei praedi. catorem, quia nec potuisset aduersus legem et prophetas docere et hoc nomine aduersus creatorem non praemissa diuersae atque aemulae diuinitatis professione. cum ergo nihil tale scriptura significet, nisi solam uim et potestatem sermonis admirationi fuisse, facilius ostendit secundum creatorem docuisse illum, quia non negauit, quam aduersus creatorem, quia non significauit. atque ita aut eius erit agnoscendus, secundum quem docuit, aut praeuaricator iudicandus, si secundum eum, aduersus quem uenerat, docuit. exclamat ibidem spiritus daemonis: quid nobis et tibi est, Iesu uenisti perdere nos; scio qui sis, sanctus dei. hic ego non retractabo, an et hoc cognomentum competierit ei, quem nec Christum uocari oporteret, si non creatoris, — alibi iam de nominibus expostulatum est — at nunc discepto, quomodo hoc eum uocari cognouerit daemon, nulla umquam retro emissa praedicatione in illum a deo ignoto et in id temporis muto, cuius nec sanctum eum contestari potuit, ut ignoti (et)iam ipsi suo creatori. quid autem iam tale ediderat nouae diuinitatis. per quod posset alterius dei sanctus intellegi? tantum quod synagogam introgressus et nec sermone operatus (erat) aliquid aduersus creatorem? sicut ergo quem ignorabat nullo modo poterat Iesum et sanctum dei agnoscere, ita quem norat agnouit. nam et prophetam meminerat sanctum dei praedicasse et Iesum nomen domini esse in filio Naue. haec et ab angelo exceperat secundum nostrum euangelium: propterea quod in te nascetur uocabitur sanctum, filius dei, et uocabis nomen eius Iesum. sed et habebat utique sensum aliquem dominicae dispositionis — licet daemon tamen — magis quam alienae et nondum satis cognitae. nam et praemisit: quid nobis et tibi, Iesu? non quasi in extraneum, (sed) ad quem pertinent spiritus creatoris. nec enim dixit: \'quid tibi et nobis\'? sed \'quid nobis et tibi\'? se deplorans et sorti suae exprobrans. quam iam uidens adicit: uenisti perdere nos. adeo iudicis et ultoris et, ut ita dixerim, saeui dei filium agnouerat Iesum, non optimi illius, et perdere et punire nescientis. quorsum hunc locum praemisimus? ut Iesum et a daemone non alium doceamus agnitum et a semetipso non alium confirmatum quam creatoris. \'atquin\', inquis, \'increpuit illum Iesus). plane, ut inuidiosum et in ipsa confessione petulantem, ut male adulantem, quasi haec esset summa gloria Christi, si ad perditionem daemonum uenisset et non potius ad hominum salutem, qui nec discipulos de subactione spirituum, sed de candida salutis gloriari uolebat. aut cur eum increpuit? si quasi mentitum in totum, ergo non fuit Iesus nec dei sanctus omnino; si quasi ex parte mentitum, quod eum legum quidem et sanctum dei, sed creatoris, existimasset, iniustissime increpuit hoc sentientem, quod sciebat sentiendum, et hoc non aestimantem, quod ignorabat aestimandum: alium legum et alterius dei sanctum. quodsi uerisimiliorem statum non habet increpatio nisi quem nos interpretamur, iam ergo et daemon nihil mentitus est, non ob mendacium increpitus; ipse enim erat Iesus, praeter quem alium daemon agnouisse non poterat, et Iesus eum confirmauit, quem agnouerat daemon, dum non ob mendacium increpat daemonem.
pass_a_gloss: In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius, He proposes that He descended into the city of Galilee, Capharnaum, certainly from the heaven of the Creator, into which He had previously descended from His own. What order was there, then, that He should first be described as descending from His own heaven into the Creator's? Why should I not also reprehend these things, which do not fulfill the faith of ordinary narration, always failing in falsehood? Let what was once said be enough, through which we have already elsewhere retracted: whether, descending through the Creator, and indeed against Him, He could have been admitted by Him and sent from there into the earth, equally His own. Now, however, I demand the rest of the order of the descent, holding that He descended. For it is seen, wherever 'appeared' is placed. To appear suddenly, from the unexpected, has the flavor of a sudden sight, which, once it has struck the eyes on what appeared without delay, seems to have descended, and it subjects the eyes to the fact. And it also makes an order and thus compels one to demand what kind of habit, what kind of suggestion, with what impetus or temperament, and also at what time of day or night He descended; furthermore, who saw Him descending, who reported it, who confirmed the thing, which is not easily to be believed even by one confirming it. It is finally unworthy that Romulus, indeed, had Proculus as a witness to his ascension into heaven, but Christ did not find an announcer of His descent from heaven, as if He did not ascend in the same ladders of falsehood as He descended. What, then, does Galilee have to do with them? If it was not the Creator's, to whom this region was destined for the entrance of preaching, saying through Isaiah: 'This first, drink quickly, region of Zabulon and land of Nepthalim, and the rest who are by the sea, and the Jordan, Galilee of the nations. A people who sit in darkness, see a great light; who inhabit the land, sitting in the shadow of death, a light has arisen upon you?' But, indeed, it is well that the God of Marcion is also vindicated as the illuminator of the nations, so that He ought to have descended, even from heaven, rather into Pontus than into Galilee. Moreover, both in place and in the work of illumination, according to the preaching, those who encounter Christ, we begin to recognize Him as having been prophesied, showing in His first entrance that He came, not to dissolve the law and the prophets, but rather to fulfill them. For Marcion has erased this as an addition. But in vain will he deny that Christ said what He immediately did in part. For He fulfilled the prophecy meanwhile, concerning the place, immediately, to the synagogue, as it is said: 'to what we have come, let us do this.' Marcion: take away also that from the Gospel: 'I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel,' and: 'it is not to take the bread of the sons and give it to the dogs,' lest Christ seem to be of Israel. The deeds are enough for me in place of words. Take away the voices of my Christ: the things will speak. Behold, He comes into the synagogue: certainly to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. Behold, He offers the bread of His doctrine first to the Israelites: certainly, that He prefers the sons. Behold, He does not impart it to others: certainly, that He passes over the dogs. To whom, however, would He have imparted it more than to the strangers of the Creator, if He Himself were not first of the Creator? And yet, how could He have been admitted into the synagogue, so sudden, so unknown, whose no one was yet certain about the tribe, about the people, about the house, about the census, finally, of Augustus, which the Roman archives keep as a most faithful witness of the Lord's birth? They certainly remembered, unless they knew He was circumcised, that He was not to be admitted into the holy of holies. But even if the synagogue was entered in a disorderly manner, nevertheless, one did not teach unless he was well-known and explored and proven long before, either in this or commended from elsewhere with this duty. They were all amazed, however, at His doctrine. Certainly, because the word was in His power, not because He taught against the law and the prophets. For the divine eloquence, indeed, presented both the power and the grace, rather building up than destroying the substance of the law and the prophets. Otherwise, they would not have been amazed, but would have been horrified, and would not have marveled, but would have immediately turned away from the destroyer of the law and the prophets, and certainly, in the first place, from the preacher of another God, because He could not have taught against the law and the prophets, and this name, against the Creator, not having been previously professed, a diverse and rival divinity. Since, therefore, the Scripture does not signify anything of this kind, except that the power and the authority of the word were for admiration, it more easily shows that He taught according to the Creator, because it does not deny it, than against the Creator, because it does not signify it. And thus, either He is to be recognized as belonging to the one according to whom He taught, or He is to be judged as a transgressor, if He taught according to the one against whom He came. The spirit of the demon cries out there: 'What is there between us and you, Jesus? You have come to destroy us; I know who you are, the holy one of God.' Here I will not retract, whether this cognomen also suited Him, whom it was not fitting to call Christ, if not of the Creator, — this has already been demanded elsewhere concerning the names — but now I dispute how the demon recognized Him by this name, with no preceding preaching having been sent out about Him from the unknown God, and at that time, when He could not have been attested as holy by the unknown God, so that He was also unknown to His own Creator. What, then, had He already brought forth of the new divinity, by which He could have been understood as the holy one of another God? Only that, having entered the synagogue, and not having worked anything in word against the Creator? Just as, therefore, the one whom He did not know could not have recognized Jesus as the holy one of God in any way, so the one whom He knew recognized Him. For the demon also remembered that the holy one of God had been prophesied as a prophet, and that Jesus was the name of the Lord in the son of Nun. He had also received this from the angel, according to our Gospel: 'Therefore, because He will be born in you, He will be called holy, the son of God, and you will call His name Jesus.' But he also had some sense of the Lord's disposition — although he was a demon — rather than of an alien and not yet sufficiently known one. For he also said beforehand: 'What is there between us and you, Jesus?' not as if to a stranger, but to one to whom the spirits of the Creator pertain. For he did not say: 'what is there between you and us?' but 'what is there between us and you?' lamenting himself and reproaching his own fate. Which, seeing, he adds: 'You have come to destroy us.' So, he recognized Jesus as the son of the judge and the avenger, and, so to speak, of the severe God, not of the good one, who does not know how to destroy and punish. Why have we premised this passage? So that we may teach that Jesus was recognized by the demon, and not by another, and confirmed by Himself, and not by another, as the Creator's. 'But,' you say, 'Jesus rebuked him.' Certainly, as one who was envious and petulant, even in his confession, as one who was flattering badly, as if this were the greatest glory of Christ, if He had come to the destruction of the demons, and not rather to the salvation of men, who did not want His disciples to glory in the subjection of spirits, but in the pure glory of salvation. Or why did He rebuke him? If as one who had lied entirely, then Jesus was not the holy one of God at all; if as one who had lied in part, because he had considered Him to be the holy one of God, indeed, but of the Creator, He rebuked him most unjustly, feeling what He knew was to be felt, and not estimating what He ignored was to be estimated: another holy one of the laws and of another God. But if the rebuke does not have a more probable status, unless we interpret it as we do, then the demon has not lied at all, not rebuked because of falsehood; for He was Jesus, apart from whom the demon could not have recognized another, and Jesus confirmed the one whom the demon had recognized, while not rebuking the demon because of falsehood.

choices.why: the phrase 'sanctus dei' is a title for Jesus
the word 'daemon' refers to an unclean spirit
the word 'propheta' refers to one who speaks for God
the name 'Iesus' is the Latin form of the name of Christ

pass_b_english: In the fifteenth year of Tiberius' reign, Luke proposes that Jesus descended into Capernaum, a city of Galilee—specifically from the Creator's heaven, into which he had previously descended from his own. What possible logic required him to be described first as descending from his own heaven into the Creator's? Why should I not also condemn these details, which fail to meet the basic credibility of ordinary narrative, always collapsing into falsehood? Let the points already made suffice, since we have retracted them elsewhere: whether, descending through the Creator and against him, Jesus could have been admitted by him and transmitted from there into the earth, equally the Creator's own. Now, however, I demand the rest of the descent's sequence, granting that he descended. For the text is clear wherever 'he appeared' is placed. To appear suddenly and unexpectedly suggests a sudden sight—one that strikes the eyes on an object that manifests without delay—whereas 'to descend' implies a process, visible as it happens, subjecting the eyes to the fact. This sequence compels the question: in what guise, with what bearing, with what force or restraint, and at what hour of day or night did he descend? Furthermore, who saw him descend, who reported it, who confirmed it—a thing not easily believed even from a confirmer? It is finally unworthy that Romulus had Proculus to witness his ascent into heaven, yet Christ found no announcer for his descent from heaven—as if he did not ascend the same ladders of falsehood by which he descended.

What business did Marcion's god have with Galilee? If it was not the Creator's—the region destined for the entrance of preaching, as Isaiah says: 'Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations. The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light; those who dwelt in a land of deep darkness, on them has light shone' (Isaiah 9:1-2)—then it is fitting that Marcion's god is vindicated as illuminator of the nations, so that he ought to have descended, even from heaven, rather into Pontus than into Galilee. Yet in both place and the work of illumination, according to the prophecy, we begin to recognize Christ as the one prophesied, showing in his first entrance that he came not to dissolve the law and the prophets but to fulfill them. Marcion erased this as an addition. But in vain will he deny that Christ said what he immediately did in part. For he fulfilled the prophecy concerning the place at once: from heaven, to the synagogue—as the saying goes, 'to what we have come, let us do this.' Marcion: take that from the Gospel too: 'I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel' (Matthew 15:24), and: 'It is not right to take the children's bread and throw it to the dogs,' lest Christ appear to belong to Israel. Deeds are enough for me in place of words. Strip away the voices of my Christ: the facts will speak. See, he enters the synagogue: precisely to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. See, he offers the bread of his teaching first to Israelites: precisely preferring the children. See, he does not yet impart it to others: precisely passing over the dogs. To whom, however, would he have imparted it more than to strangers of the Creator, if he himself were not first of the Creator?

And yet, how could he have been admitted to the synagogue—so sudden, so unknown, with no one yet certain of his tribe, people, house, or finally the census of Augustus, which the Roman archives preserve as a most faithful witness of the Lord's birth? They certainly remembered that unless they knew he was circumcised, he was not to be admitted into the holy of holies. But even if the synagogue was freely accessible, one did not teach unless well known, examined, and proven long before, either in that role or commended from elsewhere with that duty. Yet all were amazed at his teaching. Naturally—because his word had authority, not because he taught against the law and the prophets. For divine eloquence displayed both power and grace, building up rather than destroying the substance of the law and the prophets. Otherwise they would not have been amazed but horrified; they would not have marveled but turned away immediately from a destroyer of the law and the prophets, and first of all from a preacher of another god, since he could not have taught against the law and the prophets in the Creator's name without a prior profession of a rival divinity. Since Scripture signifies nothing of the sort—only that the power and authority of his word caused amazement—it more easily shows he taught according to the Creator, because it does not deny it, than against the Creator, because it does not indicate it. Thus either he is to be acknowledged as belonging to the one according to whom he taught, or judged a fraud if he taught according to the one against whom he came.

The demon's spirit cries out there: 'What have you to do with us, Jesus? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are—the Holy One of God.' Here I will not revisit whether this title suits him, whom it would not befit to call Christ if not of the Creator—that has been demanded elsewhere concerning names—but now I dispute how the demon recognized him by this name, with no prior preaching sent out about him from the unknown God, at a time when he could not have been attested as holy by the unknown God, so that he was unknown even to his own Creator. What had he already produced of the new divinity by which he could be understood as the Holy One of another God? Only that he entered the synagogue and worked nothing in word against the Creator? Just as the one he did not know could not have recognized Jesus as the Holy One of God in any way, so the one he knew recognized him. For the demon also remembered that the Holy One of God had been prophesied as a prophet, and that Jesus was the name of the Lord in the son of Nun. He had also received this from the angel, according to our Gospel: 'Therefore the child to be born will be called holy, the Son of God, and you shall call his name Jesus.' But he also had some sense of the Lord's disposition—though a demon—rather than of an alien and not yet sufficiently known one. For he also said beforehand: 'What have we to do with you, Jesus?' not as to a stranger, but to one to whom the spirits of the Creator pertain. For he did not say, 'What have you to do with us?' but 'What have we to do with you?'—lamenting himself and reproaching his own fate. Which, seeing, he adds: 'You have come to destroy us.' So he recognized Jesus as the son of the judge and avenger, and, so to speak, of the severe God—not of the good one, who does not know how to destroy and punish. Why have we premised this passage? So that we may teach Jesus was recognized by the demon, and by no other, and confirmed by himself, and by no other, as the Creator's.

'But,' you say, 'Jesus rebuked him.' Certainly—as one envious and petulant even in his confession, flattering badly, as if this were Christ's supreme glory: that he came for the destruction of demons rather than the salvation of men, who did not want his disciples to glory in the subjection of spirits but in the pure glory of salvation. Or why did he rebuke him? If for lying entirely, then Jesus was not the Holy One of God at all; if for lying in part, because the demon considered him the Holy One of God but of the Creator, he rebuked him most unjustly—punishing him for feeling what he knew must be felt, and not estimating what he did not know to estimate: another holy one of another God's laws. But if the rebuke has no more probable basis unless we interpret it as we do, then the demon has not lied at all, not rebuked for falsehood; for he was Jesus, apart from whom the demon could not have recognized another, and Jesus confirmed the one the demon recognized, while not rebuking the demon for falsehood.
